title: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way
gist: NASA's Artemis rework helps SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon landers but shifts burdens onto Lockheed Martin's Orion: it must fly backward to the Moon docked to Starship (requiring ESA/Airbus tank changes and certification for about 0.8 to 1 g of reversed load), and it must survive about two weeks in low-Earth orbit for the 2027 Artemis III docking demo. Lockheed says it is working three shifts on a zero-margin schedule.

insights.claim: NASA restructured Artemis so SpaceX's Starship lander docks with Orion in Earth orbit and travels to the Moon in tandem, while Blue Origin's Blue Moon meets Orion in low-lunar orbit, giving the lander providers more flexibility at Orion's expense.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The architecture change shifts integration risk and engineering work onto Lockheed Martin's Orion program.
insights.locator: The moves were designed to give

insights.claim: Under the new plan SpaceX fuels a Starship lander in low-Earth orbit and docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit; the crew flies on Orion and two of four astronauts transfer to Starship to land.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Starship orbital refueling remains on the critical path for crewed lunar landings.

insights.claim: Docked to Starship, Orion must fly backward to the Moon with its Service Module on top, so ESA and prime contractor Airbus are modifying the Service Module propellant tanks because liquid propellant would migrate toward the gas inlets.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Unplanned hardware modifications for Airbus/ESA add cost and schedule risk to Starship-based Artemis missions.
insights.quote: “When you push it the other way, the liquid goes to the gas end of the tank, and you don’t want the liquid in the gas part,”

insights.claim: With Starship providing translunar injection thrust, Orion would experience roughly 0.8 to 1 g of acceleration in the opposite direction, versus about 0.1 to 0.15 g in its original design, requiring new structural certification.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Requalifying Orion's structure is a concrete technical gate that could slip Starship-based lunar missions.
insights.locator: NASA and Lockheed engineers have also been studying

insights.claim: Because Orion was built for cold deep space, a roughly two-week stay in low-Earth orbit for Artemis III creates overheating risk, so some of its silver charge-dissipating thermal tape will be removed and electrical loads managed to protect avionics and cabin.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Mission-specific modifications show the Artemis III rescope is not a cheap or simple test flight.

insights.claim: NASA and Lockheed have not finished assessing orbital-debris (MMOD) risk for Orion's low-Earth-orbit Artemis III profile; the assessment is due by January and could force changes to Orion's orbit.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Watch the January debris assessment as a near-term catalyst for Artemis III mission changes.
insights.quote: “It’ll be higher risk than flying out to the Moon.”

insights.claim: NASA removed the lunar landing from Artemis III, making it a low-Earth-orbit rendezvous and docking demonstration with both landers, now targeted for summer or fall 2027, compressing integration work originally planned to be spread across missions.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A compressed 2027 docking demo raises slip risk; a delay would push out lander milestones for SpaceX and Blue Origin.
insights.quote: “It was going to be spaced out, so all that work gets crunched into this time frame.”

insights.claim: Docking Orion to Starship or Blue Moon involves mechanical hooks, connectors and pins, thruster-plume damage risk from hot or abrasive exhaust, and possible misreading of reflections by Orion's laser system.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Multiple interface risks mean the docking demo is a real technical hurdle, not a formality.

insights.claim: Lockheed Martin's Orion team is working three shifts on what its program manager calls an already zero-margin schedule to hold a 2027 Artemis III launch.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Zero schedule margin implies high probability of slips and cost growth for the Orion program.
insights.quote: “We had a zero-margin schedule already, so we’re, I call it hand-to-hand combat.

insights.claim: Lockheed's Orion program manager, a veteran of NASA during the Challenger and Columbia accidents, backs the urgency of the Moon race with China but warns against cutting corners on safety.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Tension between schedule pressure from the China race and safety culture is a source of policy and program risk.
